question.worked_solution:
Let $u=3x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=\frac{1}{3}(u-1).$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $-1/3$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $1$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}9x\sqrt{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & =9{\int }_{-1/3}^{0}\frac{u-1}{3}\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={(\frac{1}{5/2}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{1}{3/2}{u}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & ={(\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{5}\cdot {1}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {1}^{3/2})-(\frac{2}{5}\cdot {0}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {0}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =-\frac{4}{15}\end{aligned}
$$
